QUESTION 257Interview essentials
# q283

What are convention plugins?

Say this in the interview

Convention plugins package shared build rules such as Java settings, testing or quality tools for reuse across projects. They reduce repeated script fragments and make build policy reviewable. Keep them focused and avoid surprising hidden side effects.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Test shared build behavior where it is substantial. Changes can affect many modules, so versioning and compatibility matter in larger organizations.

Example / implementation sketch
java-service-conventions applies toolchain, test platform and standard task configuration.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why prefer conventions over copied build blocks?
  • What is the blast radius of a shared plugin change?

QUESTION 258Interview essentials
# q284

What is a version catalog?

Say this in the interview

A version catalog centralizes dependency and plugin aliases and their declared versions. It improves consistency and readability across build scripts. It does not by itself guarantee resolved dependency alignment or replace a platform/BOM and conflict resolution rules.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

A requested catalog version may be overridden during dependency resolution. Inspect the resolved graph when runtime versions differ from declarations.

Example / implementation sketch
implementation libs.spring.web // alias from catalog

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Does a catalog force the resolved version?
  • How does it differ from a BOM?

QUESTION 259Interview essentials
# q285

What is the difference between a platform and an enforced platform?

Say this in the interview

A platform contributes dependency constraints for version alignment. An enforced platform forces its versions more strongly and can affect downstream consumers. Use stronger enforcement deliberately because it can override choices that consumers need.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Library publication and application use have different consequences. Prefer understanding conflicts before adding forceful alignment to make an error disappear.

Example / implementation sketch
implementation platform('group:dependencies-bom:1.0') // illustrative coordinates

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why can enforcement surprise library consumers?
  • How do constraints differ from unconditional force?

QUESTION 260Interview essentials
# q286

How do you exclude a transitive dependency safely?

Say this in the interview

Identify why the dependency is present and whether the upstream library actually needs it, then exclude it narrowly on the relevant dependency edge. Validate runtime behavior afterward. Removing a JAR to silence a scanner can create missing-class failures.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Another dependency path can reintroduce it. Inspect the full graph and prefer a compatible upstream upgrade when possible.

Example / implementation sketch
implementation('example:library:1.0') { exclude group: 'example', module: 'unwanted' }

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why might an excluded module still appear?
  • What runtime risk does an unnecessary exclusion create?

QUESTION 261Interview essentials
# q287

Why can compileClasspath and runtimeClasspath contain different dependencies?

Say this in the interview

Compile dependencies support compilation, while runtime dependencies support execution and may include additional implementations. Configuration roles such as compileOnly and runtimeOnly affect visibility. Investigate the classpath that matches the actual failure.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

A successful compile can still fail with NoClassDefFoundError if runtime packaging omits needed classes. Check the packaged artifact as well as local tests.

Example / implementation sketch
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why can an application compile but fail at startup?
  • When is runtimeOnly appropriate?

QUESTION 262Interview essentials
# q288

What is the difference between a normal JAR and a Spring Boot executable JAR?

Say this in the interview

A normal library JAR typically contains its own classes and resources. A Spring Boot executable JAR uses a launcher and packaged dependencies to run the application. Choose the artifact task appropriate to library consumption or application deployment.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Do not assume jar and bootJar are interchangeable outputs. Inspect deployment scripts and classifiers so the intended artifact is selected.

Example / implementation sketch
./gradlew bootJar // Spring Boot application packaging when the plugin is applied

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Which artifact should a library publish?
  • Why might deploying the wrong JAR fail?

QUESTION 263Interview essentials
# q289

How do you configure JUnit 5 execution in Gradle?

Say this in the interview

Use the JUnit Platform for the relevant test task and declare compatible test dependencies. Verify test discovery instead of assuming a green build means tests ran. Configure additional test suites or source sets intentionally for integration work.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Include necessary engines for the chosen framework and inspect test reports. Name filters or task configuration can silently exclude intended tests.

Example / implementation sketch
tasks.named('test') { useJUnitPlatform() }

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do you verify that tests were discovered?
  • Why might zero tests produce a misleading green build?

QUESTION 264Interview essentials
# q290

How should CI reuse Gradle caches safely?

Say this in the interview

Cache dependencies and suitable task outputs with keys or validation that reflect the build environment. Keep credentials out of cached content and separate trusted write access where needed. Cache reuse should improve speed without bypassing correctness checks.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Remote caches are a supply and trust boundary: poisoned outputs can affect builds. Use scoped permissions and compatible task modeling.

Example / implementation sketch
Trusted builds write remote cache; other authorized builds read according to policy.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What can make a remote cache a security boundary?
  • Which data should never be stored in shared caches?

QUESTION 265Interview essentials
# q291

How do you investigate a dependency vulnerability in Gradle?

Say this in the interview

Identify the resolved vulnerable version and its introducing path, then choose a compatible upgrade or supported mitigation. Prefer managed alignment where applicable and validate behavior. A scanner finding should lead to dependency analysis, not arbitrary version forcing.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Confirm whether the changed component is actually packaged and used, while following the required remediation policy. Security updates can still introduce binary or behavioral incompatibilities.

Example / implementation sketch
./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency <module> --configuration runtimeClasspath

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why inspect resolved rather than declared versions?
  • What checks matter after overriding a managed dependency?

QUESTION 266Interview essentials
# q292

What is Gradle dependency substitution?

Say this in the interview

Dependency substitution changes which component fulfills a dependency, such as replacing a module with a local project for development. It can support composite builds, but changes resolution behavior and should be explicit and reviewable.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Substitution can hide differences between a local project and the published artifact. Validate the real published dependency path before release when it matters.

Example / implementation sketch
Replace module dependency with a local included-build project during development.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why might a local substitution hide packaging issues?
  • How does this differ from changing a version constraint?

QUESTION 267Interview essentials
# q293

How do you diagnose a Gradle build that works locally but fails in CI?

Say this in the interview

Compare JDK, Wrapper version, environment, dependency resolution, credentials and filesystem assumptions. Reproduce with the same tasks and inspect the first meaningful failure. Avoid assuming cache corruption without evidence.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Case sensitivity, missing generated files and untracked local configuration are common differences. Ensure required setup is versioned or explicitly provisioned.

Example / implementation sketch
./gradlew --version; compare CI task inputs and full failing task diagnostics.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Which local files may be missing from CI?
  • Why can case-sensitive paths expose a hidden bug?

QUESTION 268Interview essentials
# q31

What is the difference between logs, metrics and traces?

Say this in the interview

Logs record discrete events, metrics summarize numeric behavior over time, and traces follow a request across services. Use them together with correlation IDs to connect symptoms such as high latency to the specific slow dependency or error.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Instrument with OpenTelemetry and export to your chosen backend. Track latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Keep metric labels low-cardinality: unique request IDs belong in logs or traces, not metric labels.

Example / implementation sketch
// Metric labels: route=/payments, outcome=success
// Trace/log fields: trace_id, span_id, request_id
// Avoid customer IDs or unique request IDs in metric labels.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why is high cardinality expensive?
  • How do you propagate trace context over messaging?

QUESTION 269Interview essentials
# q32

How do you investigate high latency in a Spring Boot service?

Say this in the interview

Check latency percentiles, request rate, errors and saturation, then inspect slow traces. Separate application work from database, broker and downstream latency. Correlate changes with deployments before choosing a fix.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Look at thread pools, connection pools, GC pauses, CPU throttling and slow queries. Averages hide tail latency, so examine p95/p99 and affected routes. Reproduce the bottleneck with a representative workload and measure the fix.

Example / implementation sketch
// Compare p50 / p95 / p99 by route.
// Follow a slow trace into DB and downstream spans.
// Check pool utilization, JVM GC and container throttling.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why can p99 rise while average latency stays stable?
  • What would thread-pool exhaustion look like?

QUESTION 270Interview essentials
# q53

What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO and an error budget?

Say this in the interview

An SLI measures service behavior, such as the proportion of successful requests. An SLO sets the target for that measure over a defined window. The error budget is the allowed amount of unreliability, helping teams balance feature delivery with reliability work.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Define good events, eligible events, measurement points and exclusions carefully. For a 99.9% success SLO, 0.1% of eligible requests may fail during the window. Burn-rate alerts detect how quickly the budget is being consumed; latency SLOs need their own thresholds and event definitions.

Example / implementation sketch
// Request-based availability example:
SLI = successful eligible requests / all eligible requests
SLO = 99.9% over a rolling 30-day window
Error budget = 0.1% of eligible requests

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why are burn-rate alerts useful?
  • How would you define a latency SLI?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 271Interview essentials
# q104

How should you design useful alerts for a backend service?

Say this in the interview

Alert on actionable user impact and imminent saturation rather than every isolated error. Use service-level indicators, error-budget burn rates and suitable windows to reduce noise. Each alert should identify an owner, the affected service and a practical investigation or recovery path.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Combine fast and slow windows when appropriate to detect both severe incidents and sustained degradation. Separate paging alerts from lower-priority notifications. Validate that alerts detect real failures without routinely firing on harmless deployment transitions or expected traffic patterns.

Example / implementation sketch
Page: sustained elevated error-budget burn affecting users
Investigate: growing queue lag near a processing deadline
Dashboard only: isolated handled retry with no user impact
Every alert: owner + context + runbook

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why can a CPU threshold be a poor paging signal?
  • How do you test whether an alert is actionable?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 272Interview essentials
# q105

What is distributed tracing sampling and what are its tradeoffs?

Say this in the interview

Sampling keeps a subset of traces to control telemetry cost and volume. Head sampling decides early; tail sampling decides after observing a trace and can retain interesting outcomes such as errors or high latency. Tail sampling needs buffering and trace-aware routing, and neither approach guarantees every incident is captured.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Use consistent sampling decisions across services so traces remain useful. Tail sampling policies need bounded memory, timing and failure behavior; long traces or missing spans can complicate decisions. Keep aggregate metrics independent enough to detect problems that sampled traces may miss.

Example / implementation sketch
Head sampling: decide at request start → propagate decision
Tail sampling: collect spans → evaluate outcome → retain/drop
Metrics: track full traffic/error rates where practical

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why can head sampling miss rare errors?
  • What infrastructure does tail sampling require?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 273Interview essentials
# q106

How do you trace asynchronous messages across services?

Say this in the interview

Inject trace context into message metadata when publishing and extract it when consuming. Create producer and consumer spans, and use links when a simple parent-child relationship does not describe batching or multiple causes. Add message identifiers to logs without creating high-cardinality metric labels.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Long queue delays and retries affect trace interpretation. Distinguish enqueue time, processing time and total business completion time. A redelivery may represent another processing attempt, so preserve event identity and record attempt information without pretending every attempt is a new business operation.

Example / implementation sketch
Producer span → inject traceparent into message headers
Broker holds message → consumer extracts context
Consumer span → process → log event_id and attempt
Batch processing → use span links where appropriate

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would you represent a batch built from several messages?
  • How do you distinguish queue delay from processing latency?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 274Interview essentials
# q294

What are the four golden signals of monitoring?

Say this in the interview

Latency, traffic, errors and saturation summarize important service behavior. Use them together to distinguish demand changes from failures or capacity limits. Add business signals that reflect whether the service is accomplishing its purpose.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Aggregate success can hide a failing route or customer segment. Slice metrics with useful bounded labels rather than high-cardinality identifiers.

Example / implementation sketch
API dashboard: request rate, p95/p99 latency, error ratio, pool/CPU saturation.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why examine saturation with latency?
  • Which business signal complements payment API metrics?

QUESTION 275Interview essentials
# q295

Why are percentiles more informative than average latency?

Say this in the interview

Averages can hide slow requests experienced by a minority of users. Percentiles describe the latency distribution, such as p95 or p99. Use them with counts and time windows to understand the reliability of the estimate.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Percentiles should not generally be averaged across instances. Histograms can support suitable aggregation when buckets and queries are designed appropriately.

Example / implementation sketch
Monitor p50, p95 and p99 per relevant route alongside request volume.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why not average p99 from several pods?
  • How does low traffic affect percentile interpretation?

QUESTION 276Interview essentials
# q296

How do counters, gauges and histograms differ?

Say this in the interview

Counters accumulate events, gauges represent a current value and histograms record a distribution of observations. Choose the metric type that matches the question. For counters, account for process resets when computing rates.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Histograms need suitable bucket boundaries for useful latency queries. A gauge of the last request latency cannot describe the full latency distribution.

Example / implementation sketch
Counter: requests; gauge: active connections; histogram: request duration.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why use a rate function for a counter?
  • What happens when histogram buckets are poorly chosen?

QUESTION 277Interview essentials
# q297

What is metric cardinality and why does it matter?

Say this in the interview

Cardinality is the number of distinct label combinations that create metric time series. Unbounded labels such as request IDs or customer IDs can make telemetry expensive and unreliable. Use bounded operational dimensions and keep unique identifiers in logs or traces.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Even individually small label sets multiply when combined. Review route normalization and dynamic exception text before making them labels.

Example / implementation sketch
route=/payments/{id}, outcome=success; not route=/payments/unique-customer-id.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do labels multiply time-series count?
  • Why normalize route paths?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 278Interview essentials
# q298

How do structured logs help troubleshooting?

Say this in the interview

Structured logs store consistent fields such as timestamp, level, service, trace ID and outcome. They support reliable search and correlation compared with parsing arbitrary text. Keep sensitive data redacted and preserve useful exception context.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Logging every payload can create cost and exposure without improving diagnosis. Choose events that explain state changes and failures.

Example / implementation sketch
{level: ERROR, event: payment_failed, trace_id: ..., error_code: ...}

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Which fields should be consistent across services?
  • Why avoid logging full payment payloads?

QUESTION 279Interview essentials
# q299

What is the difference between an error log and an error metric?

Say this in the interview

An error log records details of an individual event. An error metric summarizes counts or rates for alerting and trends. Use stable error categories for metrics and attach unique request context to logs or traces.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Repeated retries can inflate counts if semantics are unclear. Distinguish failed attempts from failed user operations.

Example / implementation sketch
Metric: payment_failures_total{code="provider_timeout"}; log: operation_id + diagnostic context.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Should retries count as separate business failures?
  • Why keep unique operation IDs out of metric labels?

QUESTION 280Interview essentials
# q300

How does trace context propagate over HTTP?

Say this in the interview

A caller injects supported trace context headers and the receiver extracts them to relate spans. Instrument inbound and outbound clients consistently. Trace context is diagnostic metadata and should not be trusted as authorization or customer identity.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Missing instrumentation or proxies that drop headers can break trace continuity. Sampling decisions also need compatible propagation.

Example / implementation sketch
Producer HTTP client injects traceparent → downstream server creates related span.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What can cause a disconnected trace?
  • Why is trace context not an authorization token?

QUESTION 281Interview essentials
# q301

What makes a span useful?

Say this in the interview

A useful span represents a meaningful timed operation with clear service context, status and relevant bounded attributes. It helps identify where time and errors occur. Avoid creating excessive spans for trivial internal operations or adding sensitive payloads.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Error conventions and attribute names should be consistent. Span duration does not automatically distinguish queue waiting from active execution unless instrumented accordingly.

Example / implementation sketch
Span: database query or provider request; attributes: operation and safe target metadata.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • When are too many spans counterproductive?
  • What sensitive attributes should be avoided?

QUESTION 282Interview essentials
# q302

How do you investigate connection-pool exhaustion?

Say this in the interview

Check active, idle and waiting connections plus acquisition timeout rates. Look for slow queries, long transactions, leaked resources and total demand across replicas. Increasing pool size without checking database capacity can worsen the bottleneck.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Correlate wait time with traces and transaction duration. Separate inability to connect from connections being held too long.

Example / implementation sketch
Pool near limit + growing waiters → inspect transaction/query latency and concurrency.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why can a larger pool reduce throughput?
  • How do you distinguish leaks from slow legitimate work?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 283Interview essentials
# q303

How do you distinguish CPU saturation from CPU throttling?

Say this in the interview

Saturation means CPU demand is high relative to available execution capacity. Throttling means enforced quotas are limiting execution, potentially even when node-wide CPU is available. Inspect application CPU, container limits and throttling signals together.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Tail latency can rise when a container repeatedly exhausts its CPU quota. Compare changes with workload and limit settings before adjusting resources.

Example / implementation sketch
High quota throttling + rising p99 → inspect container CPU limit and workload profile.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Can throttling happen on an otherwise idle node?
  • Which metrics should be compared?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 284Interview essentials
# q304

How do you monitor a JVM service?

Say this in the interview

Track heap and non-heap memory, garbage collection pauses, allocation rate, threads and process CPU alongside request outcomes. JVM signals explain symptoms but should connect to latency, errors or capacity. Container limits and native memory also matter.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

A healthy heap does not rule out native memory pressure. Use profiling or recordings when aggregate metrics cannot explain the issue.

Example / implementation sketch
Request p99 + GC pauses + allocation rate + container memory + thread activity.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why monitor memory beyond heap?
  • When would you capture a JFR recording?

QUESTION 285Interview essentials
# q305

What is the difference between symptom and cause alerts?

Say this in the interview

Symptom alerts indicate user-visible failure, such as elevated error rates. Cause alerts indicate contributing conditions, such as near-full storage. Page for actionable impact or imminent failure, and avoid treating every low-level fluctuation as an incident.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Cause signals remain valuable in investigation and predictive alerts. Clear ownership and thresholds determine whether an alert is useful.

Example / implementation sketch
Symptom: failed payments; cause candidate: database pool wait spike.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why can cause-only alerting miss incidents?
  • When should a capacity signal page before impact?

QUESTION 286Interview essentials
# q306

How do you avoid alert fatigue?

Say this in the interview

Remove unactionable alerts, tune windows and thresholds, route by ownership and consolidate correlated symptoms. Distinguish paging from informational notifications. Review noisy alerts after incidents rather than asking responders to ignore them indefinitely.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Suppression should not hide distinct failures. Measure alert usefulness and maintain runbooks with concrete first checks.

Example / implementation sketch
Alert review: actionable? owned? deduplicated? correct urgency? tested?

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What makes a page actionable?
  • How do you prevent maintenance from generating misleading alerts?

QUESTION 287Interview essentials
# q307

How do you design a service dashboard?

Say this in the interview

Start with user outcomes, request volume, latency and errors, then show saturation and dependency health. Provide clear release markers and links to relevant traces and logs. A dashboard should answer operational questions rather than display every available metric.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Use consistent windows and units. Add queue age or business completion metrics for asynchronous services where HTTP success is not the final outcome.

Example / implementation sketch
Overview → affected routes → dependency breakdown → traces/logs → business state.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Which panel should an operator see first?
  • Why can HTTP 202 rates misrepresent business completion?

QUESTION 288Interview essentials
# q308

How do you observe an asynchronous business workflow?

Say this in the interview

Track durable operation states and completion deadlines in addition to technical spans. Correlate events with a stable business ID and monitor pending age, failure rate and reconciliation outcomes. A successful enqueue is not a completed business operation.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Trace retention may be shorter than the workflow lifecycle. Keep audit and recovery state in the business system rather than relying on telemetry as the source of truth.

Example / implementation sketch
operation_id → accepted → processing → completed/failed/uncertain; alert on overdue states.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why is a queue acknowledgement not business completion?
  • What state should survive telemetry expiration?

QUESTION 289Interview essentials
# q309

What are exemplars in metrics useful for?

Say this in the interview

Exemplars associate selected metric observations with trace context so an operator can jump from a latency or error signal to a representative trace. They improve diagnosis but do not mean every observation has a retained trace.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Support depends on instrumentation, export and backend configuration. Sampling and retention can make some referenced traces unavailable.

Example / implementation sketch
Latency histogram observation → exemplar trace reference → inspect slow request.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do exemplars connect metrics and traces?
  • Why might the referenced trace be unavailable?

QUESTION 290Interview essentials
# q310

How do you measure observability overhead?

Say this in the interview

Compare resource usage, latency and telemetry volume with controlled instrumentation settings. Watch high-cardinality labels, verbose logs, excessive spans and exporter queues. Keep useful diagnostic coverage while bounding cost and failure impact.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Export failures should not block critical request processing indefinitely. Define buffering, dropping and retry behavior for telemetry independently of business delivery guarantees.

Example / implementation sketch
Measure CPU/memory/p99 + exported bytes + dropped telemetry during representative load.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What should happen when a telemetry backend is unavailable?
  • How can verbose logging affect application latency?

QUESTION 291Interview essentials
# q33

How would you design a payment processing system?

Say this in the interview

Start with correctness, throughput and failure requirements. Use an authenticated API with idempotency, a durable payment state machine and a ledger. Integrate providers asynchronously where useful, and reconcile outcomes when timeouts leave the final result uncertain.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Define state transitions, audit records and unique constraints. Use an outbox for reliable event publication and idempotent handlers. Plan retries, reconciliation, refunds, access control and observability. Do not assume a timeout means the payment failed.

Example / implementation sketch
CREATED → PROCESSING → SUCCEEDED
                     → FAILED
                     → UNKNOWN → reconciliation
// Ledger and state changes need explicit transactional guarantees.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do you handle a provider timeout after charging?
  • How do you prevent duplicate payments?

QUESTION 292Interview essentials
# q34

How would you design a rate limiter?

Say this in the interview

Choose the scope, limit and burst behavior first. A token bucket supports controlled bursts; a sliding window gives a rolling count. In a distributed deployment, coordinate updates atomically in shared storage such as Redis and define behavior when that storage fails.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Keys may represent a user, client or endpoint. Consider hot keys, expiry, clock behavior and multiple regions. Return HTTP 429 with useful retry guidance. A local limiter is fast but does not enforce a global quota across instances.

Example / implementation sketch
// Atomic operation: refill tokens, then consume one if available.
// key = clientId + route
// reject → HTTP 429 + Retry-After

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why must refill and consume be atomic?
  • Would you fail open or fail closed?

QUESTION 293Interview essentials
# q35

How do you choose between SQL and NoSQL?

Say this in the interview

Start with access patterns, consistency requirements and transaction boundaries. SQL works well for relational data and multi-row transactions. NoSQL systems offer different data models and scaling tradeoffs; choose the specific database based on its guarantees.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Avoid the blanket claim that NoSQL is eventually consistent or SQL cannot scale. Compare indexes, query patterns, partitioning, durability, operational cost and consistency levels. For a financial ledger, explicit transactional integrity is usually central.

Example / implementation sketch
// Model the most important queries and invariants first.
// Evaluate transaction scope, indexes and partition keys.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would you choose a partition key?
  • What does CAP mean during a network partition?

QUESTION 294Interview essentials
# q54

What are common cache invalidation strategies and their tradeoffs?

Say this in the interview

Cache-aside loads data on a miss and usually invalidates the cache after updating the source of truth. TTL bounds staleness but does not prevent every race. Choose invalidation rules based on consistency requirements, update frequency and whether stale data is acceptable.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

A concurrent reader can repopulate an old value around an update and invalidation. Consider versioned entries, event-driven invalidation or bypassing the cache for correctness-critical reads. Protect against stampedes using request coalescing, jittered expiry or stale-while-revalidate where suitable.

Example / implementation sketch
value = cache.get(key);
if (value == null) {
    value = database.load(key);
    cache.put(key, value, ttl);
}
// Simplified cache-aside read; concurrent misses need coordination.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What causes a cache stampede?
  • Can delete-after-write still produce stale cache data?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 295Interview essentials
# q55

What is optimistic locking and when would you use it?

Say this in the interview

Optimistic locking detects conflicting updates using a version field or another comparison token. An update succeeds only if the stored version still matches the version that was read. It works well when conflicts are relatively rare; callers must handle conflicts explicitly.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

JPA supports version fields with @Version. A failed update normally requires rollback and a fresh transaction before retry. Retry only when business semantics allow it, and re-read current state before recomputing the change. Hotly contended records may need a different concurrency strategy.

Example / implementation sketch
@Entity
class Payment {
    @Id Long id;
    @Version Long version;
    String status;
}
// A stale version causes an optimistic locking failure.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • When would you choose pessimistic locking?
  • Why is blindly retrying an update unsafe?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 296Interview essentials
# q56

How should you approach a system design interview?

Say this in the interview

Clarify the main use cases, scale and reliability requirements first. Estimate traffic and storage, define the API and data model, then sketch the main components. Spend the remaining time on the hardest constraints, failure scenarios and tradeoffs rather than naming as many technologies as possible.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Confirm what must be strongly consistent, what may be asynchronous and which operations dominate traffic. State assumptions explicitly and revise them when the interviewer adds constraints. Explain why each component exists, and finish with observability, security, bottlenecks and an achievable path for growth.

Example / implementation sketch
1. Requirements: use cases, constraints, SLOs
2. Estimates: traffic, storage, peak load
3. API + data model
4. Components + request flow
5. Failure handling + tradeoffs

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do you decide what to discuss in depth?
  • What assumptions would you clarify for a banking API?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 297Interview essentials
# q57

How do you estimate capacity for a backend service?

Say this in the interview

Estimate average and peak requests per second, read/write ratio, payload size and retention. Translate these into storage, bandwidth and concurrent work. Use estimates to identify likely bottlenecks, then validate with realistic load tests and leave headroom for failures and traffic spikes.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Little’s Law relates average in-flight work to throughput multiplied by average time in a stable system. Tail latency and bursts still matter for sizing. Count replication, indexes and backups separately from raw data, and check downstream connection or request limits before assuming replicas solve capacity.

Example / implementation sketch
10 million requests/day ≈ 116 requests/second average
10× peak assumption ≈ 1,160 requests/second
At 200 ms average latency: ≈ 232 requests in flight at peak
// Estimates require workload validation and headroom.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How does latency affect the amount of concurrent work?
  • Which storage overheads are easy to overlook?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 298Interview essentials
# q58

How would you design a URL shortening service?

Say this in the interview

Expose an API that stores a long URL against a unique short code, plus a fast redirect endpoint. Use a unique constraint or conditional insert to prevent code collisions. Cache popular mappings, define expiry and custom-alias rules, and process analytics asynchronously so redirects remain fast.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Random codes need sufficient entropy and collision retries; encoded sequential IDs can reveal activity and are enumerable. Validate destinations and manage abuse. Choose redirect status and cache policy based on whether destinations can change, since browser-cached redirects can bypass later server checks.

Example / implementation sketch
POST /links  { "url": "https://example.com/page" }
Response: { "code": "a7K2p9" }
GET /a7K2p9 → lookup mapping → HTTP redirect
// UNIQUE(code); define expiry and redirect cache policy.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would you generate collision-resistant codes?
  • How would you handle a suddenly popular link?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 299Interview essentials
# q59

How would you design a reliable notification service?

Say this in the interview

Accept notification requests durably, queue delivery work and use separate workers for email, SMS or push providers. Track delivery state, retry transient failures with backoff and deduplicate requests. Respect user preferences and rate limits, and send exhausted failures to a reviewable dead-letter queue.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

A provider accepting a message is not proof that the recipient received it. Use provider callbacks where supported and authenticate those callbacks. A timeout after provider acceptance can cause duplicate sends unless the provider supports idempotency. Define ordering, priority, retention and opt-out behavior explicitly.

Example / implementation sketch
Request → durable notification record + outbox
Outbox relay → channel queue → provider worker
Provider callback → delivery-state update
// Idempotency key + bounded retries + DLQ.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do you avoid duplicate messages after a timeout?
  • How do you separate provider acceptance from delivery?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 300Interview essentials
# q60

How would you prevent double booking in a reservation system?

Say this in the interview

Enforce availability in the database using an atomic conditional update, unique constraint or suitable locking strategy. A read-then-write availability check alone is unsafe. For a temporary reservation, create an expiring hold and coordinate payment with an idempotent workflow and explicit confirmation states.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Overlapping time ranges need a stronger invariant than a unique resource ID, such as a suitable database exclusion constraint or serialized allocation logic. A payment may succeed after a hold expires, so define reconciliation and refund rules. Expiry processing must compete safely with confirmation, using conditional state transitions.

Example / implementation sketch
UPDATE seats
SET status = 'HELD', hold_id = :holdId, expires_at = :expiry
WHERE id = :seatId AND status = 'AVAILABLE';
// Proceed only if exactly one row was updated.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What if payment succeeds after the hold expires?
  • How would you prevent overlapping time-slot reservations?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 301Interview essentials
# q61

How would you design a bank transfer between two accounts?

Say this in the interview

Validate and authorize the request, deduplicate it using an idempotency key and record balanced ledger entries. Within one transactional database, update the transfer and its ledger atomically. For separate systems, use a durable workflow with reconciliation and explicit pending states rather than claiming one local transaction covers everything.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Use exact monetary representations with explicit currency and rounding rules. Protect sufficient-funds checks against concurrent spending, lock accounts in a consistent order if using row locks, and preserve an immutable audit trail. Do not claim a timeout means failure; expose a status endpoint and reconcile uncertain outcomes.

Example / implementation sketch
BEGIN;
-- Check idempotency and funds with concurrency protection.
-- Record balanced debit/credit entries and transfer state.
-- Write an outbox event in the same transaction.
COMMIT;
// Across databases: use a recoverable workflow instead.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would two simultaneous transfers avoid overspending?
  • How do you reconcile an uncertain external transfer?

QUESTION 302Interview essentials
# q62

What does the CAP theorem mean in a distributed system?

Say this in the interview

When a network partition occurs, a distributed system cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and availability for every request. A design may reject or delay some operations to preserve consistency, or accept operations with weaker guarantees. The choice depends on the operation and its correctness requirements.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

CAP consistency means a single up-to-date view consistent with real-time ordering, not the C in ACID. CAP availability means a response from every non-failing node, not an uptime percentage. It is misleading to say “choose any two” without discussing partitions and behavior during them.

Example / implementation sketch
Partition splits two replicas:
- Preserve one-copy semantics: some requests may fail or wait.
- Serve both sides: conflicting or stale views may occur.
// Decide separately for reads, writes and business invariants.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How is CAP consistency different from ACID consistency?
  • Would you accept stale data for an account balance?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 303Interview essentials
# q63

What is the difference between strong and eventual consistency?

Say this in the interview

Strong consistency commonly means reads behave as though operations occurred against one current copy, with the precise guarantee stated explicitly. Eventual consistency allows temporary differences between replicas but converges when updates stop. Choose based on which business decisions can tolerate stale data and which require coordinated state.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Consistency has more options than two labels: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, causal consistency and snapshot isolation provide different guarantees. A user may need immediate confirmation of their own update even if public counts lag. State exactly which operations require a guarantee and how the system enforces it.

Example / implementation sketch
Payment authorization: coordinate against authoritative state.
Search index / dashboard totals: controlled lag may be acceptable.
After a user writes: route a read to a source that sees that write.
// Define the guarantee per operation.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How can you provide read-your-writes with replicas?
  • Which parts of a banking application can tolerate lag?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 304Interview essentials
# q64

What is the difference between database replication and sharding?

Say this in the interview

Replication keeps copies of the same data for resilience and possibly read scaling. Sharding splits data across partitions to distribute storage and workload. They solve different problems and are often combined. Sharding introduces routing, cross-shard query and transaction challenges that replication alone does not solve.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Choose a shard key that distributes load while keeping common operations local. Tenant or customer keys may create hot shards for very large customers. Replica lag affects freshness, and failover guarantees depend on the replication and acknowledgement protocol. Plan resharding and recovery before the system reaches its limits.

Example / implementation sketch
Shard A: customers 1–N → primary + replicas
Shard B: customers N+1–M → primary + replicas
// Sharding divides the dataset; replication copies each shard.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would you choose a shard key?
  • What happens when one customer becomes a hot shard?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 305Interview essentials
# q65

What is consistent hashing and when is it useful?

Say this in the interview

Consistent hashing maps keys and nodes into a hash space so that adding or removing a node moves a limited portion of keys. It is useful for distributed caches and partition routing. Virtual nodes improve distribution, but they do not by themselves solve hot keys, replication or consistency.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

With ordinary hash(key) modulo nodeCount, changing nodeCount can remap much of the dataset. Consistent hashing minimizes this redistribution but still requires data movement, failure detection and ownership coordination. A single extremely popular key may need replication or application-level load spreading.

Example / implementation sketch
hash(key) → position on ring
Owner = next node clockwise
Node joins → takes part of a neighbor’s key range
// Virtual nodes spread ownership; hot keys still need attention.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why use virtual nodes?
  • How would you handle a single extremely hot key?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 306Interview essentials
# q66

What are CQRS and event sourcing, and do they have to be used together?

Say this in the interview

CQRS separates the models used to change state from those used to read it. Event sourcing stores domain events as the authoritative history and derives current state from them. They can be used independently. Adopt them when their audit, workflow or query benefits justify the added operational complexity.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Asynchronous read projections can lag, so users need clear expectations after writes. Event sourcing requires event schema evolution, replay safety, projection rebuilding and careful handling of sensitive data retention. A normal audit log is not necessarily an event-sourced system, and CQRS does not require separate databases.

Example / implementation sketch
Command → validate invariant → append event
Event stream → projection → read model
Query → read model
// This combines the patterns; either can also exist separately.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do you evolve old events safely?
  • How would a user read their update before a projection catches up?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 307Interview essentials
# q67

How do you make a distributed lock safe when a worker pauses?

Say this in the interview

Use a lease with an owner token and release it only if the token still matches. For correctness-sensitive writes, also use a monotonically increasing fencing token that the protected resource checks. A paused worker may resume after its lease expires, so a lock alone cannot prevent stale writes.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Lease renewal and expiration do not stop a stalled process from running again. The resource must reject operations with older fencing tokens; that enforcement cannot be delegated solely to the worker. Prefer database constraints or transactions when they can enforce the invariant more simply.

Example / implementation sketch
Worker A gets fencing token 41; pauses past lease expiry.
Worker B gets token 42 and writes to the resource.
Worker A resumes with token 41 → resource rejects stale token.
// Resource persists and enforces the latest accepted token.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why is a random ownership token different from a fencing token?
  • When is a database constraint simpler than a distributed lock?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 308Interview essentials
# q68

How do you decide between synchronous and asynchronous communication?

Say this in the interview

Use synchronous calls when the caller needs an immediate result and can tolerate the dependency’s latency and availability. Use asynchronous messaging to buffer bursts, decouple processing and support work that can complete later. Async adds delivery, ordering, deduplication and status-tracking responsibilities.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

A queue relocates waiting; it does not eliminate capacity limits. Bound backlog, monitor consumer lag and define what acceptance means. An HTTP 202 response should identify a durable operation and provide a way to check its state. Avoid turning every simple interaction into an event workflow.

Example / implementation sketch
POST /reports → persist job → return 202 + Location: /jobs/123
Worker processes durable queued job.
GET /jobs/123 → PENDING / RUNNING / COMPLETED / FAILED
// Accept only after the work is durably recorded.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What does HTTP 202 guarantee in your design?
  • How do you prevent a queue backlog from growing forever?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 309Interview essentials
# q69

What is backpressure and how do you handle an overloaded service?

Say this in the interview

Backpressure prevents producers from overwhelming consumers by controlling how much work is admitted or requested. Use bounded queues, concurrency limits and appropriate demand signals. When capacity is exhausted, reject, defer or shed lower-priority work explicitly instead of allowing memory, threads and latency to grow without bounds.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Reactive demand works within compatible pipelines but does not automatically limit every external system. An unbounded executor or broker backlog can still accumulate work. Coordinate admission control with deadlines, per-client fairness, retries with jitter and downstream capacity; return suitable retry guidance when rejecting requests.

Example / implementation sketch
if (!permits.tryAcquire()) {
    return serviceBusyWithRetryGuidance();
}
try {
    return processWithinDeadline(request);
} finally {
    permits.release();
}
// Limit both active work and queued work.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How is backpressure different from rate limiting?
  • Why can retries make an overload worse?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 310Interview essentials
# q70

How do you design for multi-region availability and disaster recovery?

Say this in the interview

Define recovery time and acceptable data loss first, using RTO and RPO. Choose active-passive or active-active deployment based on those goals and consistency needs. Plan traffic failover, data replication and dependency recovery, then test restoration and failover regularly rather than assuming replication is a complete recovery plan.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Active-active writes introduce conflict resolution and cross-region coordination tradeoffs. Asynchronous replication can lose recent acknowledged writes during failover, depending on the protocol. Backups protect against corruption and deletion scenarios that replication may copy; regularly test that backups can actually be restored.

Example / implementation sketch
RTO: target maximum recovery duration
RPO: target maximum tolerable data-loss interval
Plan: detect → fence old writer → promote → route → reconcile
// Exercise failover and backup restore against stated objectives.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why is replication not a substitute for backups?
  • How do you prevent split-brain writes during failover?

QUESTION 311Beginner
# coding-1

Filter even numbers using a Java Stream.

Say this in the interview

Use filter with a boolean predicate and collect the matching values. filter preserves the element type; it does not transform each number.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

The result of Stream.toList is unmodifiable. Preserve encounter order when the source is ordered. This solution is O(n) time plus O(k) output space.

Worked input / expected result

Input: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] Expected: [2, 4, 6]
Java solution
List<Integer> input = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6);
List<Integer> result = input.stream()
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .toList();

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Does filter change the type?
  • Is the returned list mutable?

QUESTION 312Beginner
# coding-2

Extract employee salaries with map.

Say this in the interview

Use map to transform each employee into a salary value. Use filter before map when eligibility depends on the employee.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Assume non-null employees and primitive int salaries. mapToInt is useful when the next operation is a numeric aggregate rather than a list.

Worked input / expected result

Employees: Asha=60000, Ravi=45000 Expected: [60000, 45000]
Java solution
record Employee(String name, int salary) {}
var employees = List.of(new Employee("Asha", 60000), new Employee("Ravi", 45000));
List<Integer> result = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::salary)
    .toList();

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why cannot filter extract salaries?
  • When would you use mapToInt?

QUESTION 313Intermediate
# coding-3

Find the second-highest distinct number with streams.

Say this in the interview

Remove duplicates, sort descending, skip the highest and take the next value. Return Optional because fewer than two distinct values may exist.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Sorting costs O(n log n). Distinct is important when the highest value occurs more than once. A one-pass two-value approach can be better for large inputs.

Worked input / expected result

Input: [5, 9, 9, 3, 7] Expected: Optional[7]
Java solution
var input = List.of(5, 9, 9, 3, 7);
Optional<Integer> second = input.stream()
    .distinct()
    .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())
    .skip(1)
    .findFirst();

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What if the list contains one distinct number?
  • How could you avoid sorting?

QUESTION 314Beginner
# coding-4

Find the maximum salary with mapToInt.

Say this in the interview

Map salaries to an IntStream and call max. The result is OptionalInt to represent an empty input safely.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Use long or BigDecimal for domains needing larger or exact monetary values. This example uses integer interview salaries and runs in O(n).

Worked input / expected result

Expected: OptionalInt[60000]
Java solution
record Employee(String name, int salary) {}
var employees = List.of(new Employee("Asha", 60000), new Employee("Ravi", 45000));
OptionalInt maximum = employees.stream()
    .mapToInt(Employee::salary)
    .max();

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do you handle an empty input?
  • When would int be unsuitable?

QUESTION 315Intermediate
# coding-5

Count the frequency of words with groupingBy.

Say this in the interview

Group each word by its value and use counting as the downstream collector. The resulting counts are Long values.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Decide whether case and punctuation are significant before grouping. Map iteration order is unspecified unless you supply a map factory.

Worked input / expected result

Expected mappings: java=2, sql=1 (map order unspecified)
Java solution
var words = List.of("java", "sql", "java");
Map<String, Long> counts = words.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would you ignore case?
  • How do you preserve first-seen key order?

QUESTION 316Intermediate
# coding-6

Find duplicate values using a frequency map.

Say this in the interview

Build a frequency map, retain entries whose count exceeds one and return their keys. This avoids mutable side effects inside a stream predicate.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Sorting gives deterministic output for this example. Counting is O(n) average, with extra memory proportional to distinct values; sorting duplicate keys adds cost.

Worked input / expected result

Input: [3, 1, 3, 2, 1] Expected: [1, 3]
Java solution
var input = List.of(3, 1, 3, 2, 1);
var counts = input.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));
List<Integer> duplicates = counts.entrySet().stream()
    .filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1)
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey).sorted().toList();

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why avoid a shared mutable set in filter?
  • How would you return duplicate counts?

QUESTION 317Intermediate
# coding-7

Group employees by department.

Say this in the interview

Use groupingBy with the department accessor. The collector creates a map from each department to its employees.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Decide how null department values should be handled before collecting. Supply LinkedHashMap when predictable first-seen group ordering matters.

Worked input / expected result

Expected groups: IT=[Asha, Ravi], HR=[Maya]
Java solution
record Employee(String name, String department) {}
var employees = List.of(new Employee("Asha", "IT"),
    new Employee("Ravi", "IT"), new Employee("Maya", "HR"));
Map<String, List<Employee>> groups = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::department));

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do you count employees per department?
  • What if department is null?

QUESTION 318Advanced
# coding-8

Find the highest-paid employee in each department.

Say this in the interview

Group by department and use maxBy as the downstream collector. Each group contains an Optional of its maximum employee.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

If salaries tie, a tie-breaker decides which employee wins. maxBy returns one employee, not all employees tied at the maximum.

Worked input / expected result

Expected winners: IT=Asha, HR=Maya
Java solution
record Employee(String name, String department, int salary) {}
var employees = List.of(new Employee("Asha", "IT", 60),
    new Employee("Ravi", "IT", 50), new Employee("Maya", "HR", 55));
Map<String, Optional<Employee>> top = employees.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::department,
        Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary))));

QUESTION 324Advanced
# coding-14

Find the first non-repeated character using streams.

Say this in the interview

Count code points in encounter order, then select the first whose count is one. LinkedHashMap preserves first-seen ordering for the search.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Code points handle supplementary Unicode characters better than char units, but not every user-perceived grapheme cluster. State whether case and whitespace count.

Worked input / expected result

Input: "swiss" Expected: Optional[w]
Java solution
String text = "swiss";
Map<Integer, Long> counts = text.codePoints().boxed().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
Optional<String> first = counts.entrySet().stream()
    .filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1L).map(Map.Entry::getKey)
    .findFirst().map(cp -> new String(Character.toChars(cp)));

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why preserve encounter order?
  • How do code points differ from char values?

# coding-22

Create a REST endpoint with a path variable.

Say this in the interview

Use @RestController for response-body handling, @GetMapping for the route and @PathVariable to bind a URI segment.

These annotations handle HTTP concerns, not business authorization. Explicit parameter names avoid relying on compiler metadata.

// Registers an MVC controller whose return values become response bodies.
@RestController
class PaymentController {
    // Maps HTTP GET requests to this path.
    @GetMapping("/payments/{id}")
    PaymentDto find(
        // Binds the {id} URI segment to this argument.
        @PathVariable("id") String id) {
        return service.find(id);
    }
    private final PaymentService service;
    PaymentController(PaymentService service) { this.service = service; }
}

A little deeper

Query parameters differ from path variables. Type conversion failures should produce a controlled client error.

Worked input / expected result

GET /search → limit=20; GET /search?limit=5 → limit=5.
Commented Spring Boot example
// Registers a REST controller with response-body semantics.
@RestController
class SearchController {
    // Handles HTTP GET on /search.
    @GetMapping("/search")
    String search(
        // Binds ?limit=; defaults to 20 when missing or empty.
        @RequestParam(name = "limit", defaultValue = "20") int limit) {
        if (limit < 1 || limit > 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid limit");
        return "limit=" + limit;
    }
}

record CreatePayment(
    // Requires a non-null, non-whitespace account value.
    @NotBlank String accountId,
    // Rejects null; @DecimalMin alone allows null.
    @NotNull
    // Requires amount >= 0.01.
    @DecimalMin("0.01") BigDecimal amount) {}

// REST controller: serialize return values into HTTP bodies.
@RestController
class CreateController {
    // Matches HTTP POST /payments.
    @PostMapping("/payments")
    // Uses 201 Created for a successful return.
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    CreatePayment create(
        // Triggers validation of the bound DTO.

        // Deserializes the HTTP request body.

}

// Registers this configuration class.
@Configuration
class Clients {
    // Registers a bean named primaryClient.

    RestClient primary(RestClient.Builder b) { return b.baseUrl("https://primary.example.com").build(); }
    // Registers a bean named backupClient.

    RestClient backup(RestClient.Builder b) { return b.baseUrl("https://backup.example.com").build(); }
}
// Registers the business-service component.
@Service
class Reader {

        // Selects backupClient instead of the other RestClient bean.
        @Qualifier("backupClient") RestClient client) {}
}

    @Transactional(rollbackFor = IOException.class)

# coding-33

Cache reads and evict entries after updates.

Say this in the interview

Use @Cacheable for cache lookups and @CacheEvict for invalidation, with caching enabled. Cache keys and freshness rules must match the domain.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Proxy self-invocation can bypass caching advice. Cache eviction is not a universal cure for concurrent stale repopulation.

Worked input / expected result

Scenario: repeated reads reuse a cached product; successful update evicts that ID.
Commented Spring Boot example
// Registers configuration.
@Configuration
// Enables Spring cache interception; configure the intended CacheManager.
@EnableCaching
class CacheConfig {}

// Registers the business service.
@Service
class ProductService {
    // Returns a cached value for id, or caches the method result on a miss.
    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#id")
    public Product find(String id) { return load(id); }
    // Evicts this key after a successful invocation by default.
    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", key = "#id")
    public void update(String id, Product product) { persist(id, product); }
    // load/persist implementations are omitted.
}

QUESTION 345Advanced
# coding-35

Execute work asynchronously with @Async.

Say this in the interview

Enable async interception, configure an executor and call an @Async method through its managed proxy. Return a future when the caller needs a completion result.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Do not use self-invocation or assume thread-local transactions follow the new task. Bound executor capacity and handle rejected or failed tasks.

Worked input / expected result

Scenario: an injected Reports proxy schedules the task on reportExecutor.
Commented Spring Boot example
// Declares configuration.
@Configuration
// Enables proxy interception of @Async methods.
@EnableAsync
class AsyncConfig {
    // Registers a named, bounded executor.
    @Bean("reportExecutor")
    ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor() {
        var e = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        e.setCorePoolSize(2); e.setMaxPoolSize(4); e.setQueueCapacity(20);
        return e;
    }
}
// Registers the async service bean.
@Service
class Reports {
    // Submits external proxy invocations to the named executor.
    @Async("reportExecutor")
    public CompletableFuture<String> generate() {
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture("report-ready");
    }
}

QUESTION 346Intermediate
# coding-36

Map a JPA entity with a generated ID and version.

Say this in the interview

Use @Entity for persistence identity, @Id for the primary key and @Version for optimistic conflict detection. Choose an ID strategy compatible with the database.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

JPA entities need an accessible no-argument constructor. @Column constraints should be applied through real schema migrations; annotations alone do not guarantee an existing database was changed.

Worked input / expected result

Scenario: conflicting updates to one versioned payment can fail optimistic locking.
Commented Spring Boot example
// Marks this class as a JPA entity.
@Entity
// Maps it to the payments table.
@Table(name = "payments")
class Payment {
    // Identifies the primary key field.
    @Id
    // Uses the database identity strategy; confirm database support.
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    Long id;
    // Tracks optimistic-lock version changes.
    @Version
    Long version;
    // Declares non-null mapping/schema metadata for this column.
    @Column(nullable = false)
    String status;
    protected Payment() {}
}

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Does @Column update a production schema automatically?
  • What happens on a stale version?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 347Intermediate
# coding-37

Write a Spring Data repository query with named parameters.

Say this in the interview

Extend the appropriate repository interface and use @Query when a derived method name is insufficient. @Param binds named JPQL parameters.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

JPQL uses entity and property names, not table and column names. Spring Data creates repository proxies; a repository interface normally does not require its own @Repository annotation.

Worked input / expected result

Input: status="PENDING" → matching Payment entities.
Commented Spring Boot example
interface PaymentRepository extends JpaRepository<Payment, Long> {
    // Defines JPQL over the Payment entity and its status property.
    @Query("select p from Payment p where p.status = :status")
    List<Payment> findByState(
        // Binds this argument to the named :status query parameter.
        @Param("status") String status);
}

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How does JPQL differ from SQL?
  • Does a Spring Data interface need @Repository?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 348Intermediate
# coding-38

Fetch a relationship explicitly with @EntityGraph.

Say this in the interview

Use an entity graph to describe relationships to fetch for a repository operation. This helps avoid lazy N+1 queries when the endpoint needs the relationship.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

The attribute must exist on the mapped entity. Inspect SQL and pagination behavior; fetching everything eagerly is not a general performance solution.

Worked input / expected result

Scenario: load orders and their customers for a DTO without one extra query per order.
Commented Spring Boot example
interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    // Requests fetching the mapped customer relationship for this operation.
    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer")
    List<Order> findByStatus(String status);
}
// Assumes Order defines a mapped customer association and status property.

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What causes N+1 queries?
  • Why inspect SQL after adding an entity graph?

QUESTION 349Intermediate
# coding-39

Test MVC request mapping with @WebMvcTest.

Say this in the interview

Use @WebMvcTest for a focused MVC slice and replace service collaborators with the supported mock-bean mechanism for your framework version.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

This example assumes Spring Framework 6.2+ @MockitoBean and Boot 3.x imports. Boot 4 may reorganize testing packages. Security filters and dependencies still need deliberate test setup.

Worked input / expected result

Scenario: test HTTP validation/serialization without starting database infrastructure.
Commented Spring Boot example
// Loads an MVC slice for this controller, not the whole application.
@WebMvcTest(PaymentController.class)
class PaymentControllerTest {
    // Injects the slice-provided HTTP test client.
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    // Replaces/adds the Spring-context collaborator with a Mockito mock.
    @MockitoBean PaymentService service;
    // Declares a JUnit 5 test method.
    @Test
    void mappingExample() throws Exception {
        // Configure service behavior and security as required by the endpoint.
    }
}

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What does this slice not test?
  • How is @MockitoBean different from @Mock?

QUESTION 350Intermediate
# coding-40

Test the complete Spring application context.

Say this in the interview

Use @SpringBootTest when full application wiring is required. A random port starts an embedded server for real HTTP calls, unlike a focused slice.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Provide test database, broker and secret configuration. @ActiveProfiles selects test configuration but does not make external side effects safe by itself.

Worked input / expected result

Scenario: verify complete wiring against controlled test dependencies.
Commented Spring Boot example
// Loads the full Boot context and starts a server on a random available port.
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
// Activates test-specific configuration.
@ActiveProfiles("test")
class ApplicationTest {
    // Declares the integration test method.
    @Test
    void contextStarts() { /* assert a meaningful application invariant */ }
}

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why is this slower than a slice?
  • Does a test profile automatically isolate all external systems?
