QUESTION 351Beginner
# coding-41

Select employees earning more than 60,000.

Say this in the interview

Filter rows with WHERE and use an explicit ORDER BY for deterministic output.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

SQL result ordering is not guaranteed without ORDER BY. This example assumes salary is a non-null integer.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, salary Expected rows: [1, "Asha", 90000] [3, "Maya", 90000] [2, "Ravi", 70000] [6, "Noor", 70000]
SQL solution
SELECT id, name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 60000
ORDER BY salary DESC, id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why specify a tie-breaker?
  • How would NULL salaries behave?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 352Intermediate
# coding-42

Find the second-highest distinct salary in SQL.

Say this in the interview

Find the maximum salary below the overall maximum. Duplicates of the highest salary do not count as a second distinct value.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

The aggregate returns one row with NULL when no second distinct salary exists. This differs from returning no rows.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: second_highest Expected rows: [70000]
SQL solution
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What if all salaries are equal?
  • How would DENSE_RANK solve this?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 353Intermediate
# coding-43

Find every employee with the third-highest distinct salary.

Say this in the interview

Use DENSE_RANK over salary descending, then filter the rank in an outer query.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

DENSE_RANK preserves ties without rank gaps. ROW_NUMBER would pick positions, not distinct salary levels.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, salary Expected rows: [4, "Dev", 60000] [8, "Isha", 60000]
SQL solution
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, name, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank
  FROM employees
)
SELECT id, name, salary FROM ranked
WHERE salary_rank = 3 ORDER BY id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How does RANK differ?
  • What if fewer than three salary levels exist?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 354Advanced
# coding-44

Return the top two salary levels in each department.

Say this in the interview

Partition DENSE_RANK by department and keep ranks up to two. All employees tied within those levels are included.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

This deliberately returns two distinct salary levels, not exactly two employees. Employees without a department are excluded.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, department_id, salary Expected rows: [1, "Asha", 10, 90000] [2, "Ravi", 10, 70000] [6, "Noor", 10, 70000] [3, "Maya", 20, 90000] [4, "Dev", 20, 60000] [8, "Isha", 20, 60000] [5, "Leela", 30, 50000]
SQL solution
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, name, department_id, salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r
  FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT id, name, department_id, salary FROM ranked
WHERE r <= 2 ORDER BY department_id, salary DESC, id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would you return exactly two employees per department?
  • Why exclude null departments?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 355Intermediate
# coding-45

Count employees in every department, including empty departments.

Say this in the interview

LEFT JOIN from departments and count the non-null employee ID.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

COUNT(*) counts the outer join’s placeholder row for an empty department. COUNT(e.id) gives zero instead.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, employee_count Expected rows: [10, "Engineering", 3] [20, "Finance", 3] [30, "HR", 1] [40, "Sales", 0]
SQL solution
SELECT d.id, d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS employee_count
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name ORDER BY d.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why not COUNT(*)?
  • What changes with an INNER JOIN?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 356Beginner
# coding-46

List employees with their department, preserving unassigned employees.

Say this in the interview

LEFT JOIN from employees so an employee without a matching department remains in the result.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Conditions on the right table placed in WHERE can unintentionally remove unmatched rows. Keep join and filtering semantics explicit.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, department Expected rows: [1, "Asha", "Engineering"] [2, "Ravi", "Engineering"] [3, "Maya", "Finance"] [4, "Dev", "Finance"] [5, "Leela", "HR"] [6, "Noor", "Engineering"] [7, "Arun", null] [8, "Isha", "Finance"]
SQL solution
SELECT e.id, e.name, d.name AS department
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id
ORDER BY e.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What if department_id has no matching row?
  • How can WHERE change the outer join behavior?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 357Intermediate
# coding-47

Find employees who have no matching department.

Say this in the interview

Use a LEFT JOIN and select rows where the joined department ID is NULL.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

This finds both unassigned employees and non-matching foreign-key references if the schema allows them. A foreign-key constraint can prevent invalid references.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name Expected rows: [7, "Arun"]
SQL solution
SELECT e.id, e.name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id
WHERE d.id IS NULL ORDER BY e.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would NOT EXISTS express this?
  • Does department_id IS NULL find invalid non-null references?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 358Intermediate
# coding-48

Find employees earning above their department average.

Say this in the interview

Compare salary with an average computed over the employee’s department.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

This correlated subquery excludes employees with a null department under SQL null comparison rules. A window-function approach can also compute averages.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, salary Expected rows: [1, "Asha", 90000] [3, "Maya", 90000]
SQL solution
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2
  WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id
) ORDER BY e.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would a window function help?
  • Why are unassigned employees excluded?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 359Beginner
# coding-49

Return all employees tied for the highest salary.

Say this in the interview

Compare each salary to a scalar MAX aggregate rather than limiting to one row.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

ORDER BY plus a one-row limit can silently omit tied winners. State whether the interview wants one winner or all ties.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, salary Expected rows: [1, "Asha", 90000] [3, "Maya", 90000]
SQL solution
SELECT id, name, salary FROM employees
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)
ORDER BY id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why not fetch only the first sorted row?
  • How do you add a deterministic single-winner policy?

QUESTION 360Beginner
# coding-50

Find salary values shared by more than one employee.

Say this in the interview

Group by salary and filter aggregate counts with HAVING.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

WHERE filters source rows before grouping; HAVING filters grouped results. Choose columns that are valid under the grouping rules.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: salary, occurrences Expected rows: [90000, 2] [70000, 2] [60000, 2]
SQL solution
SELECT salary, COUNT(*) AS occurrences
FROM employees
GROUP BY salary HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY salary DESC;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why use HAVING instead of WHERE here?
  • How would you return the employees themselves?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 361Intermediate
# coding-51

Show each employee alongside their manager name.

Say this in the interview

Self-join employees using manager_id and preserve top-level employees with a LEFT JOIN.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Use distinct aliases to separate employee and manager roles. This query shows one level, not an entire recursive management hierarchy.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, employee, manager Expected rows: [1, "Asha", null] [2, "Ravi", "Asha"] [3, "Maya", null] [4, "Dev", "Maya"] [5, "Leela", null] [6, "Noor", "Asha"] [7, "Arun", null] [8, "Isha", "Maya"]
SQL solution
SELECT e.id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How would you return an entire reporting hierarchy?
  • Why use LEFT JOIN rather than INNER JOIN?

QUESTION 362Intermediate
# coding-52

Find customers who have never placed an order.

Say this in the interview

Use NOT EXISTS to exclude customers for whom an order exists.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

NOT EXISTS avoids the null trap that can affect NOT IN when the subquery returns null. An index on orders.customer_id may help.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name Expected rows: [4, "Dev"]
SQL solution
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
) ORDER BY c.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • What is the NOT IN null trap?
  • Which index might support this query?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 363Intermediate
# coding-53

Calculate each customer’s paid spend, including zero spend.

Say this in the interview

LEFT JOIN paid orders and use COALESCE on SUM so customers with no paid orders show zero.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Keep the paid-status condition in the join. Moving it into WHERE would remove customers whose matching paid rows do not exist.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, paid_total Expected rows: [1, "Asha", 300] [2, "Ravi", 0] [3, "Maya", 80] [4, "Dev", 0]
SQL solution
SELECT c.id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS paid_total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'PAID'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why put status in ON?
  • Why is COALESCE needed?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 364Intermediate
# coding-54

Find customers whose paid spend exceeds 150.

Say this in the interview

Filter paid orders, group them by customer and use HAVING on SUM.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

This query does not need zero-spend customers. If joining more one-to-many tables, avoid multiplying order amounts through duplicate joined rows.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, paid_total Expected rows: [1, "Asha", 300]
SQL solution
SELECT c.id, c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS paid_total
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 150
ORDER BY c.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How can joining order_items inflate this sum?
  • When would you aggregate before joining?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 365Advanced
# coding-55

Find the most recent order for each customer.

Say this in the interview

Use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by customer and ordered by date descending, with ID as a tie-breaker.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

A deterministic tie-breaker selects one winner when dates match. Customers without orders are absent unless joined back from customers.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, customer_id, status, created_at Expected rows: [2, 1, "PAID", "2025-02-05"] [3, 2, "PENDING", "2025-01-20"] [5, 3, "CANCELLED", "2025-02-22"]
SQL solution
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, customer_id, status, created_at,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT id, customer_id, status, created_at FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY customer_id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do you include customers without orders?
  • Why include id in the window ordering?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 366Advanced
# coding-56

Calculate a running paid total per customer.

Say this in the interview

Use SUM as a window function with an explicit ordered ROWS frame.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

A window aggregate keeps individual rows instead of collapsing them. The explicit frame and tie-breaker prevent ambiguous peer handling.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, customer_id, amount, running_paid Expected rows: [1, 1, 100, 100] [2, 1, 200, 300] [4, 3, 80, 80]
SQL solution
SELECT id, customer_id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
    ORDER BY created_at, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_paid
FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID'
ORDER BY customer_id, created_at, id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How is this different from GROUP BY?
  • Why specify ROWS and a tie-breaker?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 367Intermediate
# coding-57

Calculate paid revenue by calendar month.

Say this in the interview

Derive a month key, group paid orders by it and sum amounts.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

The example uses ISO text dates and SUBSTR for the shared dataset. Production timestamp grouping should use the database’s date functions and an explicit business time zone.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: month, revenue Expected rows: ["2025-01", 100] ["2025-02", 280]
SQL solution
SELECT SUBSTR(created_at, 1, 7) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID'
GROUP BY SUBSTR(created_at, 1, 7) ORDER BY month;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why does time zone matter for real timestamps?
  • How would you include months with no revenue?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 368Beginner
# coding-58

Select orders in January using a half-open date range.

Say this in the interview

Use an inclusive lower bound and an exclusive start-of-next-month upper bound.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Half-open ranges avoid end-of-day timestamp mistakes. The shared dataset uses ISO text dates; production queries should bind correctly typed date or timestamp parameters.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, created_at Expected rows: [1, "2025-01-10"] [3, "2025-01-20"]
SQL solution
SELECT id, created_at FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01'
  AND created_at < '2025-02-01'
ORDER BY created_at, id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • Why avoid an upper bound of January 31 at midnight?
  • How can functions on a date column affect index use?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 369Intermediate
# coding-59

Count paid and pending orders for every customer.

Say this in the interview

Use conditional aggregation over a LEFT JOIN and count only rows matching each status.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

Each CASE returns zero for unmatched or other-status rows. Include all relevant statuses explicitly if a complete reconciliation is needed.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, name, paid_count, pending_count Expected rows: [1, "Asha", 2, 0] [2, "Ravi", 0, 1] [3, "Maya", 1, 0] [4, "Dev", 0, 0]
SQL solution
SELECT c.id, c.name,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'PAID' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'PENDING' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending_count
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do cancelled orders affect these counts?
  • Why does an empty customer still have one joined placeholder row?
Chapter ↑
QUESTION 370Intermediate
# coding-60

Compute paid order totals from line items.

Say this in the interview

Join orders to their items and sum quantity multiplied by unit price for each order.

Understand it better · explanation, example & follow-ups

A little deeper

The fixture assumes exact integer amounts in one currency. Real systems need explicit decimal or minor-unit rules, currency and rounding. An inner join excludes orders without lines.

Worked input / expected result

Using the shared SQL dataset. Columns: id, line_total Expected rows: [1, 100] [2, 200] [4, 80]
SQL solution
SELECT o.id, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS line_total
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID'
GROUP BY o.id ORDER BY o.id;

Be ready for these follow-ups

  • How do you include orders without line items?
  • Why should currencies not be mixed in one sum?
